opus-5.5.text:
I think there's a common misconception that being good at math means being fast, like the person who can multiply big numbers in their head or solve a competition problem in ten minutes. Speed helps in certain settings, but I don't think it's the core of it.

For me, a few things matter much more.

The first is taste: knowing which questions are worth asking. In research you're not handed a well-posed problem with a guaranteed answer. You're wandering through a huge space of possible statements, and the people I admire most have a sense for which direction is fertile and which is a dead end. That's hard to teach directly. It comes from seeing a lot of mathematics and building intuition for what "should" be true.

The second is comfort with being stuck. Most of the time, doing math means not knowing the answer, sometimes for weeks or months. Good mathematicians have a high tolerance for that discomfort. They can hold a problem in their head for a long time, come back to it from different angles, and not panic when the first ten approaches fail. Competition math trains a little of this, but research demands much more of it.

The third is the ability to move between levels: to have a vivid, almost visual intuition for why something is true, and then sit down and turn that intuition into a fully rigorous argument where every step checks out. Some people are strong on intuition but sloppy, others are very careful but can't see the big picture. The really strong ones go back and forth fluently.

And I'd add that a lot of it is just love for the subject. Mathematics rewards obsession. If you find yourself thinking about a problem in the shower or on a walk, not because you have to but because you can't help it, that's usually a good sign.

This is also part of why I find the intersection with AI so interesting. Formal verification, like proof assistants, can take over some of the "checking every step" burden. That might free humans to focus more on taste and intuition, the parts that are hardest to formalize. So the question of what makes someone good at math may itself shift over the next decade.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a question I've thought about a lot, partly because I grew up being told I was "good at math" and then spent years figuring out what that actually meant.

The honest answer is that there isn't one kind of mathematical talent. When I was doing olympiads, the thing that mattered was speed and pattern recognition under pressure. You see a problem, something clicks, you recognize a structure you've seen before in a different costume. That's a real skill, but it's a narrow one, and I think a lot of people mistake it for the whole thing.

When I got to research, I realized the people who were truly good were different. They were comfortable being confused for a very long time. Months, sometimes years, sitting with a problem that doesn't yield. The olympiad kids who burned out were often the ones who couldn't tolerate that. They were used to the feeling of being fast, and research almost never gives you that feeling.

So if I had to name the core thing, I'd say it's taste combined with stubbornness. Taste is knowing which questions are worth asking, which directions smell promising, when a proof is ugly in a way that means you're missing something. That's hard to teach and I think it's mostly absorbed from being around people who have it. The stubbornness part is more democratic. Anyone can decide to not give up.

And then there's something about abstraction that I think is underrated. Good mathematicians can hold a very compressed representation of a huge structure in their head and move pieces around without losing track. It's a little like having a good working memory for ideas rather than for numbers. People assume math is about calculation, but most of the mathematicians I admire are actually bad at arithmetic.

The last thing I'd say, and this came up a lot when we were building Axiom, is that you can decompose a lot of what looks like genius into things that are learnable, if you're willing to be honest about what the pieces are. That's not to say everyone can be Terence Tao. But the gap between a competent mathematician and someone who thinks they're "not a math person" is mostly exposure and tolerance for discomfort, not some innate wiring.

astra-6.text:
I think being good at mathematics involves several different things. There’s technical ability—being able to work through a difficult argument—but there’s also imagination, asking good questions, and being willing to stay with something you don’t understand.

People often associate mathematical ability with speed. And speed can be useful, but when you’re working on a problem where you don’t even know what the right approach is, patience matters a lot. Can you try a small example? Can you notice why your approach failed and use that to ask a better question?

I also think there’s something important about being comfortable saying, “I don’t understand this.” That gives you a place to start. Sometimes the question you’re embarrassed to ask turns out to be the question that helps everyone understand the problem more clearly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think being good at mathematics is less about being fast and more about being willing to stay with something you don’t understand. You can look at a problem and have no idea where to begin, but then you try a small example, notice a pattern, or ask a slightly different question. That curiosity matters a lot.

And you need both intuition and rigor. Intuition helps you imagine what might be true; rigor makes you ask whether you actually know why it’s true. I think a lot of growth happens in that gap—when something feels obvious, but trying to explain it reveals that you haven’t quite understood it yet.
